results.title: I stopped using free VPNs after I learned what they do with your traffic
results.author: Joe Rice-Jones
results.content:
If you type “free VPN” into any search engine, you’ll get a wall of options. They might even sound good, with promises not to log your traffic, to stop your ISP from snooping on your browsing, and other claims of private browsing.
The reality is somewhat different, from your ISP to an often unidentified entity in the middle. With most apps, that’s a downgrade, and many free VPN providers have been found to leak data accidentally or even sell your data on the dark side. Some don't even do what they say, and send your data unencrypted across the internet.
Your free VPN sees more than you think, even with HTTPS
And some apps break HTTPS on purpose
When you route your browsing traffic through any VPN, the operator sees your real IP address, every destination IP, your DNS lookups, and the plaintext hostname (SNI) from every HTTPS handshake. It can’t see the contents of encrypted pages, but they don’t need to. The metadata is more than enough to recreate your browsing habits in painstaking detail.
This also assumes the app is doing what it’s supposed to be. A CSIRO study from 2016 found that of the 283 Android VPN apps tested, 84% leaked IPv6 traffic outside the tunnel, 66% leaked DNS queries, and 18% didn’t encrypt anything at all. That's a shocking breach of trust on most accounts, and you'd hope things would be better now.
A decade later, and the picture is better but not perfect. The recent MVPNalyzer study found that 29 of the 281 free Android VPNs tested still leaked traffic, 61 sent data in plaintext, and over 80% sent data to known ad and tracking domains. Progress is slow when money is at stake.
How free VPNs actually make money
Congratulations, your PC is now the product
Servers and bandwidth cost money, even as it becomes one of the cheaper parts of hosting. A free VPN that doesn’t have a paid tier is immediately suspect, because it’s making money somehow, and you’re probably the product being sold.
Hotspot Shield’s free tier has been caught injecting JavaScript and redirecting shopping traffic through affiliate partners, which is what Honey got caught doing too. Facebook bought Onavo mostly to watch which apps you used, and app-analytics firm Sensor Tower hid a bunch of VPN and ad-block apps behind shell companies.
And more recently, Urban VPN was caught harvesting AI chats and then selling them as marketing analysis. It even kept collecting data when the VPN was turned off, and uninstalling was the only fix. I'm not saying all free VPN providers are sketchy. They're not. But the industry has a bad reputation, and it keeps being reinforced.
What you can use instead
Some free VPNs are trustworthy, but there are better options
Every trustworthy VPN with a free tier comes with three things. Open source clients, independent audits to back up their no-log claims, and paying subscribers are the reason there’s a free part at all. It’s mind-numbingly boring, and that’s how it should be.
Proton VPN Free is an XDA favorite, offering a service for one device with unlimited data, no ads, the same encryption as the paid plans, and a handful of exit node options. The paid options allow you to protect more devices at once, which can be handy.
But there are others that are worth considering. Windscribe Free gives you 10GB a month and unlimited devices. TunnelBear has published Cure53 audits every year since 2016, but its tiny data cap makes it more of a taster demo. And you could always use Tailscale or NetBird, or self-host on a VPS.
What ‘no-logs’ means when the police show up
Marketing claims are one thing, but they don’t hold up in court when the police turn up with subpoenas. Some free VPNs say they don’t log anything, but they really do, and then hand over any metadata to the authorities.
One that doesn’t is Windscribe, which was tested in court. Greek prosecutors charged the founder over traffic from a Windscribe server, and the case was dismissed, as the company had nothing to produce. That’s what you want from your VPN provider: an actual auditable architecture that doesn’t log your details.
The safest free VPN might be the one you self-host
Free VPNs aren’t automatically scams, but you should be wary of them for the most part. That’s not to say you shouldn’t be using a VPN when you use coffeeshop or hotel Wi-Fi, because you should, and be wary of any login pages that show up. You can skip the worrying and self-host WireGuard on a cheap VPS, and then the only person using it is you
The only thing there is that you’re trading off the obscurity that commercial VPN providers supply for a VPN that you control. But that’s probably fine; security-by-obscurity is pretty much a meme at this point.
results.summary:
Many free VPN services compromise user privacy by leaking data, tracking browsing habits, or selling personal information to third parties, necessitating caution when selecting a secure connection tool.

### Key Points
- Research from MVPNalyzer indicates that over 80% of free Android VPNs send user data to known advertising and tracking domains.
- Common security failures include leaking DNS queries, exposing IPv6 traffic, and transmitting data in plaintext without encryption.
- Providers like Urban VPN have been caught harvesting user data, including AI chat logs, even when the application is disabled.
- Trustworthy free VPNs, such as Proton VPN and Windscribe, typically feature open-source clients, independent security audits, and transparent business models.
- Self-hosting a VPN using WireGuard on a virtual private server offers a secure alternative that eliminates reliance on third-party providers.

### Why it Matters
Using unreliable free VPNs can expose sensitive metadata and browsing history to malicious actors or data brokers rather than protecting it. Choosing audited, transparent services or self-hosted solutions is essential for maintaining genuine digital privacy and security.

results.title: CargoNet reports $304.6M in losses, Scott Cornell says Q2 theft drop is no trend yet
results.author: Phil Brink
results.content:
Fewer cargo theft reports did not mean smaller losses during the second quarter, according to Verisk CargoNet's analysis. The intelligence network documented 677 incidents across the United States and Canada. That total fell 26% from Q2 2025. It also dropped 14% from the previous quarter.
Estimated cargo losses nevertheless climbed to $304.6 million during the three-month period. That figure more than doubled the $135.7 million reported during Q2 2025. The average reported commodity value reached $564,009. Several multimillion-dollar thefts involving metals and enterprise technology heavily influenced that average.
"Lower incident volume should not be mistaken for lower risk," Keith Lewis, Verisk CargoNet's vice president of operations, said. "The groups driving the largest losses are not necessarily trying to steal more freight; they are trying to identify the right shipment." Lewis pointed to metals and enterprise technology as areas attracting organized theft groups. Those shipments can offer major value and established resale opportunities.
One quarter does not establish a trend
Scott Cornell, EVP, Crime and Theft Specialist at SPG Cargo & Logistics and chair of TAPA Americas, discussed the results during a recent FreightWaves interview. He described the decrease as welcome news after years when theft activity stayed elevated. Cornell also urged the industry to avoid treating one quarter as proof of a broader shift. "It's not going to be a trend until we see it for maybe two or three quarters consecutively," Cornell said.
Cornell noted that cargo theft numbers have historically moved up and down. He said recent law-enforcement arrests could be contributing to the quarterly decrease. Those efforts included operations in New York, New Jersey, California and Canada, along with FBI and Homeland Security cases. Cornell called the results from law enforcement and private-sector cooperation encouraging.
CargoNet's data showed declines in physical thefts involving loaded equipment and non-delivery schemes. Those schemes involved bad actors acquiring established motor carriers, booking freight under their operating authority, then failing to deliver it. California and Texas recorded notable reductions in that activity. Theft classifications dropped from 488 events during Q2 2025 to 378 this year.
Fictitious pickup incidents moved far less, falling from 165 reports to 158. CargoNet also found steady activity involving business email compromise and shipment misdirection. Compromised accounts can expose shipment details, contact directories and transportation-management tools. Criminals can then impersonate trusted parties or alter load information.
results.summary:
Verisk CargoNet reports that while the total number of cargo theft incidents in the United States and Canada dropped by 26% during the second quarter, financial losses surged.

### Key Points
- Cargo theft incidents fell to 677, a 26% decrease compared to the same period in 2025.
- Total estimated losses reached $304.6 million, more than doubling the $135.7 million reported last year.
- The average value per theft rose to $564,009, driven largely by high-value shipments of metals and enterprise technology.
- Law enforcement operations in states including California, New York, and New Jersey contributed to the decline in reported incidents.
- Non-delivery schemes and physical thefts of loaded equipment saw the most significant volume reductions.

### Why it Matters
The sharp increase in total losses despite fewer incidents highlights a shift toward more targeted, high-value thefts by organized criminal groups. Industry experts warn that this quarterly data does not yet signal a long-term trend and emphasize that supply chain security remains a critical financial risk.

results.title: A Dystopian New Movie Has the Weirdest Premise Ever. Here’s Everything You’ve Wanted to Know.
results.author: Nadira Goffe
results.content:

Ever wonder what the world of The Purge would be like if the vice made legal for one day weren’t crime, but sex? I can’t say that hypothetical has ever crossed my mind, but maybe it should have, for it’s given all of us the gift of One Night Only, a buzzy new rom-com starring Monica Barbaro and Callum “Mr. Dua Lipa” Turner. Written by Travis Braun and directed by Will Gluck, a directorial veteran of the genre whose notable works include Easy A, Friends With Benefits, and Anyone but You, One Night Only is set in a version of America where a chastity “mandate” prohibits premarital or extramarital sex, except for a singular 12-hour period each year where everyone gets to get it on.
The zany premise of the film has resulted in an ongoing meme of people joking about living in a world where the big night is real. (Like Old’s “the beach that makes you old” and Challengers’ “the wind that makes you cheat,” there’s just something fun about repeating the words “the one night a year you can legally have sex.”) And yet, despite the obvious parallel to The Purge, a better comparison may be 1984, for the two stories share a fascist government that imposes an insane bevy of rules (and incentives to report rulebreakers) on its citizens in order to keep them in line. In a Reddit AMA, Gluck explained that his team “spent a lot of time talking about the rules of the world,” which he mainly relegated to the literal background in the film, merely hinted at or explained via street signs, posters, and news anchors talking on TVs during scenes. Why? Well, as he says: “We didn’t want the movie to be about that.”
What the movie is about, ostensibly, is two beautiful singles, Owen (Turner) and Allie (Barbaro), who try to navigate this world’s rules on the big night in New York City. Naturally, as any good rom-com would dictate, their paths keep unintentionally crossing until they consider whether or not they should intentionally cross them for the foreseeable future. But, in what may be a first, these attractive people’s sexy adventure time isn’t really what you want to know about. Fear not: I’m here to break down just how something as ridiculous as One Night Only’s dystopia could possibly work.
What’s this absurd-sounding sex law?
Three years before the events of One Night Only began, the United States government instituted a mandate that outlawed premarital sex, with the exception of one night (12 hours, from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m.) when premarital sex is legal. In the film, it is ingeniously dubbed and marketed as “the One Night.”
Are there any other terms or conditions?
Protection is still required even during the mandate relief, though it’s made clear that the type of protection required is specifically a condom. IUDs, birth control pills, and other contraceptives are not mentioned.
Condoms are hard to come by in the film due to the high demand, allowing the movie to stage a funny scene where Allie and Owen both run around New York, stopping by various bodegas and urgent care centers looking for a place that still has condoms available. This complication also allows for a little sponcon, as Durex is the only brand of condom shown or mentioned in the whole movie. They better have shelled out the big bucks for that!
How is this sex law possibly enforced?
The mandate is enforced by biometric trackers, made by the fictional Rexton Labs, that get implanted into the wrists of everyone over the age of 18. As explained by a tech bro played by Nicholas Braun (aka Cousin Greg from Succession), these sensors measure, in part, dopamine, serotonin, and testosterone as a way to gauge if you’re, well, engaging. When the biosensor registers a spike in levels while near another sensor that’s also spiking, it alerts law enforcement “via 5G.” (As if that weren’t enough snitching, signs in the background of the movie encourage citizens to call a hotline to report others having illegal sex.)
The biosensors take the shape of a tattoo on the wrist that glows red for unmarried people and green for married folks. Each unwed person’s red sensor turns green for the 12 hours that they are allowed to get biblical (as do the chyrons on the subways, which sport a countdown instead of the useful information about what stop is up next—thanks a lot, MTA!). The tattoo can take the shape of whatever the person desires.
What about the—
Let me stop you right there: No, it is never explained how law enforcement checks if unmarried couples having legal sex during this One Night are using condoms.
So, what if teens under the age of 18 want to have sex, as they are … kinda known to do?
I can’t stress to you enough how unanswered this very reasonable question remains.
Hilariously, what we do know is whether this sex law also applies to non-American tourists, to which the answer is: Yes. Gluck told Polygon that in a scene that ended up getting cut, they suggested that even visitors to the States would have to get a biosensor when going through immigration, but “it takes like six seconds.” Why six seconds? Why not?! Is it painless? Who knows! And wouldn’t this absolutely nuke the country’s tourism economy? That’s for other geniuses to figure out!
I presume that if you leave the country, no international law enforcement body cares or is tracking the data from your biosensor just to make sure Americans aren’t living it up elsewhere?
Correct! Allie and Owen pass promotional signs from airline companies encouraging people to fly internationally, where premarital sex is legal.
OK, I have so many questions. The biggest, though, is: Wouldn’t people just keep getting married and divorced to have sex, as a loophole?
Though it’s never stated in the film, there are signs pointing to some rules around marriage to prevent people from just getting married and divorced constantly. Gluck told Polygon that “You have to stay married for one year and one day before you can get divorced. Because if not, people would just go get married, get divorced, get married, get divorced, right?” Damn it, foiled again.
How did this mandate even come to be? Who made this happen?
In a scene showing a conservative-coded politician being interviewed on national news, he explains that “we wanted to go back to a time when sex was reserved for the sanctity of marriage.” Later, in a conversation between Owen’s mom, Linda (Molly Ringwald), and her boyfriend, Rick (LeVar Burton), Rick mentions that the bill was passed by Congress in what was likely a close vote.
As for some justification, the politician explains on air that teen pregnancies are “near zero” and the number of reported sexually transmitted infections have reached “record lows” as a result of this law. He also points to some social reasoning, including quips like: “Now it’s a badge of honor to be an incel.” This politician’s name is apparently Holloway, as indicated by a vandalized campaign poster in Allie’s apartment saying “Resist Holloway.” Vanity Fair reported that an early draft of the movie’s script includes a character named “Senator Holloway,” described as “41, beard, Botox, gives a practiced smile. He definitely does not look exactly like JD Vance.”
When asked why the government allows the rulebreaking for one night, Holloway says that “politics require compromise.” He also makes an unctuous comment about this being the thing that separates the U.S. from other countries and governments, though it’s unclear whether he’s referring to compromise generally or the One Night exception. It is clear, however, that he means it in a disgustingly nationalist way meant to infantilize other countries, especially considering he says it while being interviewed by a Chinese newscaster on a Chinese news station.
What happens if you’re caught doing the nasty without a wedding ring?
The punishment for violating the mandate and having premarital sex at any other time is never explained. At one point, Allie encounters someone who had been in prison and is currently on parole for other crimes, and thus is not allowed to have sex even on the One Night, during which his sensor stays red. However, it’s unclear whether any of his sentence was due to a previous violation of the chastity rule. Gluck told Polygon that his guess is that “if you do it many times, there’s probably fines involved, and then if you ultimately continue to do it, there’s probably some sort of jail sentence,” but the team behind the film “didn’t wanna get that far into it.”
So what is allowed outside the confines of the One Night? Are you allowed to get off at all?
In a scene that takes place at a police station, a poster using bathroom-sign-type stick-figure graphics to explain what counts as legal and illegal sex acts makes clear that masturbation and tamer forms of foreplay are legal year-round, but oral and anal sex are not and must be reserved for the One Night.
What about workarounds? Surely people have found some.
Premarital sex in the LGBTQ+ community is also outlawed under the mandate, but Allie’s roommate implies that the LGBTQ+ community has found ways to skirt the rules. These ways are, sadly, never divulged.
Naturally, as expected for any true American society in 2026, this mandate has also opened a new market. The reason Nicholas Braun’s character is exposition-dumping to Allie about how the sensors work is because he is employed at a biotech company that is working on a pill to mask the rise of the tracked chemicals so that the chips won’t detect when people are having sex. Yeah, that would definitely happen in real life.
About that—what if you’re just having a really good time with someone else? What if you’re eating the most orgasmic cookie you’ve ever had in your life alongside a friend who’s doing the same thing? What if you’re masturbating separately near someone? Could those scenarios still trigger the sensor and make it seem like you’re breaking the law by having premarital sex?
Good questions, none of which are answered or explained.
I will note that Allie has a conversation with a police officer wherein she chastises the officer for enforcing this insane law. But the officer basically tells her that cops don’t like having to run around after people checking to see if they’re having sex either. (“Where’s your conscience?” Allie asks. “With my pension,” the cop responds.) I think it’s fair to assume that in false-alarm scenarios the police still get called and realize their time (and our tax dollars) are being wasted, especially when they arrive to see people doing absolutely nothing sexual.
So, Allie doesn’t agree with the mandate. How does the general public feel?
It’s very clear that general society is not OK with this mandate. There are plenty of signs in apartments and shop windows and plastered onto exterior walls that say “REPEAL,” not to mention the graffiti and street posters that trash the mandate and rally against government surveillance. A part of the film’s plot also includes an anti-mandate concert set to take place at Radio City Music Hall.
This is kind of a dark premise for a rom-com, isn’t it?
If you think too hard about it, yes it is. Not only is it pretty severely fascist (especially considering the citizen-policing hotlines), but you also get a rundown of the number of businesses, big and small, that seek to profit on this ruling. Barbershops and bookstores are shown running One Night deals, and a Chinese restaurant is shown having a One Night special for dumplings. A fake Duolingo ad sports the phrase “Get lingual for the one night,” while other companies, like the aforementioned airlines, also attempt to get in on the action. Beyond the biotech bro’s company working to profit on public health—Allie confirms whether this research could cure Parkinson’s, to which Braun’s character says yes, but “there’s no money in that shit!”—at one point, a character walks past a business sporting a sign promoting “A.I. Sexx Booths,” suggesting there’s lots of money to be made on the margins here.
You’ve only given me more unanswered questions.
I’m sorry! I, too, wondered many things while watching, like how the A.I. booths work, whether divorce rates or sexual assault rates have skyrocketed, or if more people are stuck in deeply unhappy marriages. Someone asked me what happens to married people who practice infidelity or swinging, and I could provide no answer from the movie. There are so many world-building holes, One Night Only may as well be made of Swiss cheese.
Should I go see this movie?
One Night Only makes literally no sense at all. It involves gross bodily fluids (and not even the ones you’d expect out of a sex Purge movie). The politics are scary. There’s an incredible amount of secondhand embarrassment.
And yet, it’s perfect. Give me 10 more films just like this. The chemistry between Turner and Barbaro is palpable, the script is funny, and the movie is full of celebrity cameos. (At one point Julia Fox turns up as a bartender, and both my seat-neighbor and I laughed.) Most of all, it’s charming! I immediately wanted to rewatch it with all of my friends. One Night Only may be terrible, but it’s terrible in the best way possible.
results.summary:
The new romantic comedy *One Night Only*, starring Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner, depicts a dystopian America where premarital sex is illegal except for one annual 12-hour window.

### Key Points
- Directed by Will Gluck, the film features a government-mandated chastity law enforced by biometric wrist sensors developed by the fictional Rexton Labs.
- The plot follows two singles navigating New York City during the legal window, which is marketed as "the One Night."
- Citizens are monitored for hormonal spikes via 5G-connected sensors, with public signage encouraging neighbors to report illegal sexual activity.
- The film explores a commercialized dystopia where businesses, including airlines and biotech firms, profit from the restrictive mandate.
- Despite the absurd premise, the movie features cameos from actors like Nicholas Braun, Molly Ringwald, LeVar Burton, and Julia Fox.

### Why it Matters
The film uses a high-concept, satirical premise to explore themes of government surveillance and the commercialization of personal autonomy. By blending dystopian tropes with traditional rom-com elements, it highlights how extreme social policies can reshape both public infrastructure and private behavior.

results.title: Stocks Settle Higher as a Weak Jobs Report Allays Rate Hike Fears
results.author: Rich Asplund
results.content:
The S&P 500 Index ($SPX) (SPY) closed up +0.62% on Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ($DOWI) (DIA) closed up +0.28%, and the Nasdaq 100 Index ($IUXX) (QQQ) closed up +1.19%. September E-mini S&P futures (ESU26) rose +0.55%, and September E-mini Nasdaq futures (NQU26) rose +1.17%.
Stock indices settled higher on Friday amid strength in corporate earnings results and reduced Fed rate hike fears. Stock indices found support on Friday as bond yields fell after US July nonfarm payrolls unexpectedly declined and average hourly earnings rose less than expected, bolstering speculation that the Fed won’t be forced to raise interest rates any time soon. The 10-year T-note yield fell -3 bp to 4.65%. The payroll report cut the chances of a Fed rate hike at next month’s FOMC meeting to 44% from 58% before the report.
Atlassian surged more than +36% to lead software stocks higher today after forecasting stronger-than-expected Q1 revenue. Cybersecurity stocks also rallied on Friday, led by a 4% jump in Cloudflare after it reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings. In addition, chipmakers received support on Friday as Microchip Technology rallied more than +13% after forecasting stronger-than-expected net sales for next quarter.
US July nonfarm payrolls unexpectedly fell by -23,000, weaker than expectations of an +80,000 increase and the first decline in 5 months. June payrolls were revised downward to show a +20,000 increase from the previously reported +57,000. The July unemployment rate unexpectedly fell -0.1 to a 13-month low of 4.1%, showing a stronger labor market than expectations of no change at 4.2%.
US July average hourly earnings rose +0.1% m/m and +3.2% y/y, weaker than expectations of +0.3% m/m and +3.5% y/y.
US June consumer credit rose $14.173 billion, stronger than expectations of $11.850 billion.
Thursday evening, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said policymakers cannot afford to tolerate higher inflation and "it is crucial that monetary policy put a meaningful restraint on underlying inflation, rather than tolerating somewhat higher inflation today to pursue productivity growth tomorrow."
Sep WTI crude oil prices (CLU26) rose more than +1% on Friday as the markets await news of an Iran-Oman agreement to partially reopen the Strait of Hormuz. A joint statement from the two countries is under review, and the route would remain active for two to four months, though the agreement does not mean a full reopening, according to Iranian officials. Iran said that a normalization of the strait will depend on the US lifting its blockade on Iranian ports.
However, crude prices gave up their gains and turned lower Friday afternoon in post-market trading after Reuters reported that the US will lift its blockade of Iranian ports once a deal to reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is announced.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that Arab negotiators are concerned that Iran's diplomats may not be able to guarantee compliance with any agreement reached, as Iran's lead negotiators are under pressure from hardline officials to eke out more explicit references to Iran's role in the strait and clearer benefits. On Thursday, Iran's semi-official Fars news agency reported that vessels belonging to the US, Israel, or any other nation that has "caused damage" to Iran would be prohibited from the Strait of Hormuz under the proposed deal with Oman to reopen the waterway, which would restrict some oil exports from several Gulf States.
The outlook for strong Q2 earnings is a bullish factor for stocks. Forecasts compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence suggest Q2 earnings may increase by +23%, close to Q1’s blowout earnings of +30%, which was more than double the +12% analysts had expected. AI spending is expected to account for most of earnings, with AI infrastructure stocks set to contribute nearly 60% of the S&P 500's earnings-per-share growth in Q2. So far, earnings results have been positive, with 86% of the 440 S&P 500 companies that have reported Q2 earnings beating estimates, according to Bloomberg data.
The markets are discounting a 44% chance of a +25 bp rate hike at the next FOMC meeting on September 15-16.
Overseas stock markets settled mixed on Friday. The Euro Stoxx 50 climbed to a new all-time high and closed up +0.33%. China's Shanghai Composite rose to a 3-week high and closed up +1.02%. Japan's Nikkei-225 Stock Average closed down -0.12%.
Interest Rates
September 10-year T-notes (ZNU6) closed up +4.5 ticks on Friday. The 10-year T-note yield fell -2.4 bp to 4.654%. T-note prices rose on Friday after the Fed-friendly July payroll report showed an unexpected decline in nonfarm payrolls and a smaller-than-expected increase in average hourly earnings, bolstering speculation that the Fed won’t be forced to raise interest rates any time soon. T-notes fell back from their best level on Friday as stocks rallied, which curbed safe-haven demand for government debt securities.
European government bond yields moved lower on Friday. The 10-year German bund yield fell -0.8 bp to 3.132%. The 10-year UK gilt yield fell -1.6 bp to 4.921%.
German trade news was better than expected. German June exports rose +0.9% m/m, stronger than expectations of +0.5% m/m. Also, June imports rose +4.4% m/m, stronger than expectations of +2.0% m/m.
German June industrial production rose +0.2% m/m, right on expectations.
Markets are discounting an 85% chance of a +25 bp ECB rate hike at its next policy meeting on September 10.
US Stock Movers
Microchip Technology (MCHP) closed up more than +13% to lead chipmakers higher after forecasting Q2 net sales of $1.59 billion to $1.62 billion, well above the consensus of $1.56 billion. Also, Qualcomm (QCOM) closed up more than +4%, and Marvell Technology (MRVL), NXP Semiconductors NV (NXPI), and Analog Devices (ADI) closed up more than +3%. In addition, Nvidia (NVDA), Applied Materials (AMAT), ASML Holding NV (ASML), KLA Corp (KLAC), and Texas Instruments (TXN) closed up more than +2%.
Atlassian (TEAM) closed up more than +35% to lead software stocks higher after forecasting stronger-than-expected Q1 revenue. Also, Palantir Technologies (PLTR) closed up more than +10% and ServiceNow (NOW) closed up more than +6%. In addition, Workday (WDAY) closed up more than +5%, and Salesforce (CRM) closed up more than +3% to lead gainers in the Dow Jones industrials. Finally, Oracle (ORCL), Datadog (DDOG), and Autodesk (ADSK) closed up more than +2%, and Intuit (INTU) and Adobe Systems (ADBE) closed up more than +1%.
Mining stocks rallied on Friday amid the surge in gold and silver prices. Coeur Mining (CDE) closed up more than +10%, and Anglogold Ashanti (AU) closed up more than +9%. Also, Newmont Corp (NEM) closed up more than +7%, and Hecla Mining (HL) closed up more than +6%. In addition, Barrick Mining (B) closed up more than +5%, Southern Copper (SCCO) closed up more than +3%, and Freeport McMoRan (FCX) closed up more than +2%.
Cybersecurity stocks are rallying today, led by a +5% jump in Cloudflare (NET) after it reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings. Also, Zscaler (ZS), Okta (OKTA), and CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) closed up more than +3%, and Palo Alto Networks (PANW) closed up more than +1%.
Doximity (DOCS) closed up more than +31% after raising its 2027 revenue forecast to $671 million to $681 million from a previous forecast of $664 million to $676 million, stronger than the consensus of $672.8 million.
Twilio (TWLO) closed up more than +24% after boosting its full-year adjusted operating income forecast to $1.14 billion to $1.16 billion from a previous forecast of $1.04 billion to $1.06 billion, higher than the consensus of $1.10 billion.
Natera (NTRA) closed up more than +20% after raising its full-year revenue forecast to $2.85 billion to $2.91 billion from a previous forecast of $2.74 billion to $2.82 billion, stronger than the consensus of $2.80 billion.

Do you remember the Great Black Plastic Kitchen Utensil Scare of 2024? Even though the math was a little off in the report that ignited the movement, it pushed home cooks in the right direction of eliminating harmful chemical compounds from their kitchens. In 2026, the buzz is all about getting rid of PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” in our cookware. Yes, we’ve been aware of them for years, but as a shopping editor, I’ve only recently seen the market respond with high-quality nonstick pots and pans that rival their toxic predecessors’ ease of use.
One such piece is the Titanium Always Pan Pro from Our Place. The only thing standing between it and the top of our list of the best nonstick pans is the price—upwards of $150. But today, the handy 8.5-inch size of the nonstick, non-toxic pan is on sale for as little as $85.

But what makes the Titanium Always Pan Pro stand out from its siblings is its proprietary NoCo® Nonstick Technology that’s built right into the pan rather than coated on top of the finished product. That helps it last longer—a lifetime, with proper care—than pans with a nonstick coating, regardless of whether it contains PFAS.
What The Kitchn Team Thinks of the Titanium Always Pan Pro
Shopping writer Micki Wagner had been using classic Always Pans in her own kitchen for three years before upgrading to titanium pans. “Now they’ve become my go-to cookware,” she wrote in her Titanium Always Pan Pro review. Because it can withstand temperatures up to 1000°F, she said it’s “comparable to stainless steel cookware when it comes to searing meats and veggies, but without the learning curve and serious scrubbing” during cleanup. Her absolute favorite thing about it is the micro honeycomb pattern on the cooking surface, which enhances its nonstick-iness. I’ve been reporting on Our Place sales for years, and I don’t think I’ve ever seen a discount this good outside of a major sale event. If your old nonstick pans have seen better days, now is the time to replace them.

results.title: Farmers Are Getting Control Of Their Equipment Back
results.author: Chao Liu and Katharine Trendacosta
results.content:
Farmers Are Getting Control Of Their Equipment Back
from the right-to-repair dept
For years, John Deere had actively made repairing their tractors near-impossible for anyone but itself and the few “authorized” repair shops—regardless of the ability of its customers to actually visit such shops. Now, in a major win for farmers and right to repair advocates, John Deere must soon provide farmers with not just the tools and resources to finally repair their own John Deere equipment, but also access to future updates for said equipment.
In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) brought a suit against farm equipment manufacturer John Deere, alleging John Deere used their control over equipment repair tools and resources to limit the ability of farmers and independent repair providers (IRPs) to repair John Deere equipment. Earlier this month, John Deere reached a settlement with the FTC in which they will immediately make available a tranche of repair resources, then continue to make further resources available until the end of the year. Five states joined the FTC in this suit, and over the next 10 years these states will work alongside the FTC to ensure John Deere complies with this settlement.
It is worth noting there is a second, farmer-initiated antitrust lawsuit against John Deere, also concerning a farmer’s right to repair their own equipment. In April, John Deere agreed to a $99 million settlement in that case, which also includes right to repair provisions.
This fight is just one example of how, as machines become increasingly computerized, companies like John Deere restrict your ability to repair machines behind software subject to legal regimes that don’t just lock down repair, but make unauthorized repair a potential criminal offense.
John Deere’s market dominance in farm equipment led to an extraordinary power over access to the tools and resources of repair. John Deere actively restricted who had access to repair tools, and monopolized who could do the repair. This revenue stream—and control of it—is built into the business models of a lot of the technology we buy today. It also encourages companies to move away from the kinds of devices that can be easily fixed at home to ones that offer bells and whistles no one wants but makes repair difficult—like app-enabled toasters.
This whole saga with John Deere has been an exemplar of the greater need for right to repair laws, policy, and enforcement. There was a time when you bought a tractor and with some know-how and a manual could fix it yourself. It is easy to envision why someone with John Deere farm equipment might find it inconvenient to wait for John Deere approved repairpeople to come and fix any broken equipment. Especially when it meant waiting for days or weeks. Especially if it meant their crop was withering on the vine. This settlement will help ensure this is no longer the case.
But it’s not just about farm equipment; If you can’t fix it, you don’t own it. While some might feel more willing to agree they “shouldn’t” futz with laptops or smartphone, it still stands that — whether it’s farm equipment, a car, a laptop, or even your phone — if you legally cannot fix it yourself, if you must go hat in hand to an “approved provider,” you are at the mercy of a corporation. It is why EFF continues to support right to repair laws that ensure people truly own what they buy. And it is why EFF continues to fight for exemptions to the law that makes it most difficult to tinker and repair your own devices.
Originally published to the EFF’s Deeplinks blog.

John Deere has reached a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission to provide farmers with the necessary tools, software, and resources to repair their own agricultural equipment.

### Key Points
- The FTC settlement requires John Deere to release repair resources immediately and continue providing access through the end of 2025.
- Five states will partner with the FTC to monitor John Deere’s compliance with the repair mandate over the next decade.

### Why it Matters
This settlement marks a significant victory for the right-to-repair movement by challenging corporate control over software-locked hardware. It sets a critical precedent for consumer ownership, potentially influencing how other technology companies manage repairability for products ranging from farm machinery to personal electronics.

"The idea is to let users ask questions about an item they might be looking at," he said. If someone is looking at ingredients on their kitchen countertop, for example, they could ask Siri for dinner ideas.

results.title: Does an 'Elite' chip really matter? I put two Android flagships to the test to find out
results.author: bradypsnyder@gmail.com (Brady Snyder) , Brady Snyder
results.content:
Qualcomm is making major strides in mobile processing by introducing custom Oryon cores in a smartphone processor. Now, the generational improvements have made their way across Qualcomm's chip portfolio — even to processors that don't bear the "Elite" branding.
This makes it tricky to compare the performance capabilities across smartphone models and chip generations. For instance, Motorola's new Razr Ultra 2026 is powered by the last-generation Snapdragon 8 Elite chip. By comparison, the Razr Fold runs on a newer Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 mobile platform, just the non-Elite version.
I wanted to see whether an older Elite chip or a newer "base" chip offered better performance, so I put the Razr Ultra 2026 and the Razr Fold through a six-text benchmark gauntlet. The results weren't what I expected.
How I tested the Razr flagships
I put the Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 and the Motorola Razr Fold through a series of six tests, each designed to gauge a specific aspect of device performance. To test CPU performance, which affects how snappy your device feels when opening apps and during basic use, I used both Geekbench 6 and Geekbench 7. For on-device AI testing, I ran Geekbench AI and its TensorFlow Lite framework. To see how the phones handled gaming and graphics-based tests, I ran 3DMark's Wild Life Extreme benchmark and stress test.
I ran each benchmark test three times, starting the next run immediately after the first one finished. This provides a clean average of the results that is more representative of real-world performance than a single run. Running the benchmark trials in quick succession hints at how the Razr Ultra 2026 and the Motorola Razr Fold handle sustained loads, and whether the phones experience major thermal throttling.
After completing three runs of each benchmark test, I allowed the phones to cool down before beginning the next test. This ensures the strain of former tests isn't impacting the performance of a current test.
CPU and AI benchmark performance
The Snapdragon 8 Elite chip inside the Razr Ultra 2026 features two prime CPU cores that can be clocked up to 4.32GHz, plus six more performance CPU cores that can reach 3.53GHz. Meanwhile, the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip inside the Razr Fold is built on newer Oryon Gen 3 prime CPU cores, but they are only clocked at up to 3.8GHz. The processor's six performance CPU cores can hit up to 3.32GHz.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
So, the older Elite chip offers higher clock speeds, and the base Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip has newer prime cores. Since the two chips have the same number of prime and performance CPU cores, the Razr Ultra 2026 and the Razr Fold's benchmark results should be in the same ballpark. Let's see how they turned out.
| Geekbench 6 CPU benchmark results |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Device/chip | Test 1 | Test 2 | Test 3 | Average | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Motorola Razr Fold (Snapdragon 8 Gen 5) | 2,612 single-core / 8,809 multi-core | 2,596 single-core / 8,480 multi-core | 2,572 single-core / 8,388 multi-core | 2,593 single-core / 8,559 multi-core | 
| Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) | 2,830 single-core / 8,372 multi-core | 2,782 single-core / 8,261 multi-core | 2,762 single-core / 8,170 multi-core | 2,791 single-core / 8,268 multi-core | 
In Geekbench 6, the older Snapdragon 8 Elite chip consistently beat the newer base Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 processor by a few hundred points in single-core CPU performance. The Razr Fold averaged a 2,593 single-core score, whereas the Razr Ultra 2026 averaged a 2,791 single-core score. This kind of performance is what makes your phone feel fast when opening apps, loading webpages, or navigating the UI. Despite the Razr Ultra 2026's older chip and constrained form factor, the Elite processor still wins here.
As for multi-core performance, the Razr Fold manages to pull more out of the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5's eight CPU cores. The newer, base chip's best benchmark run resulted in a multi-core score of 8,809, and an average of 8,559. The Razr Ultra 2026 was notably behind, putting up an 8,268 multi-core score. Essentially, this means the Razr Fold's non-Elite chip will be better for multitasking and parallel workloads than the Razr Ultra 2026's older Elite chip — at least as configured here.
In terms of performance trends, each phone unsurprisingly posted its best result on the first try. However, the three CPU tests didn't cause either phone to noticeably throttle. The results for the second and third trials weren't too far off what we saw in the first run.
| Geekbench 7 CPU benchmark results |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Device/chip | Test 1 | Test 2 | Test 3 | Average | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Motorola Razr Fold (Snapdragon 8 Gen 5) | 1,082 single-core / 5,883 multi-core | 1,077 single-core / 5,935 multi-core | 1,103 single-core / 5,717 multi-core | 1,087 single-core / 5,845 multi-core | 
| Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) | 1,235 single-core / 6,787 multi-core | 1,018 single-core / 6,697 multi-core | 990 single-core / 6,848 multi-core | 1,081 single-core / 6,777 multi-core | 
Geekbench 6 is widely used for smartphone comparisons and chip benchmarking, but Geekbench 7 is here. This updated test offers "both new and improved workloads to measure the performance of your CPUs and GPUs." In other words, it's better built to test how phones and chips will handle the demanding AI and media workflows used in 2026.
The results painted a different picture. While the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip in the Razr Fold was better at multi-core performance in the Geekbench 6 test, the opposite was true using the Geekbench 7 benchmark. The older Snapdragon 8 Elite processor in the Razr Ultra 2026 posted multi-core scores as much as over 1,000 points higher than the newer Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip in the Razr Fold.
Single-core performance was about the same across the two phones and chips. The shift in multi-core performance does beg the question: Is the older Elite chip actually better-positioned for modern multitasking?
| Geekbench AI benchmark results |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Device/chip | Test 1 | Test 2 | Test 3 | Average | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Motorola Razr Fold (Snapdragon 8 Gen 5) | 4,101 quantized score | 3,726 quantized score | 3,968 quantized score | 3,932 quantized score | 
| Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) | 3,586 quantized score | 3,248 quantized score | 2,900 quantized score | 3,245 quantized score | 
If you care about on-device AI performance, it seems having a newer chip is more important than having an "Elite" one. The base Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 averaged a Geekbench AI quantized score of 3,932, whereas the Snapdragon 8 Elite was further behind with an average score of 3,245.
GPU benchmark performance
Perhaps the most surprising part of this test was seeing the difference in GPU performance between the two Motorola flagships. I used 3D Mark's Wild Life Extreme, a 4K UHD gaming benchmark, to push each phone and processor to its limits in a one-minute test. The results were clear: the older Elite chip in the Razr Ultra 2026 is better for gaming and graphics-heavy tasks.
The Snapdragon 8 Elite processor in the Razr Ultra 2026 averaged 32.36 frames per second across the three minute-long trials. Meanwhile, the Razr Fold could only muster a 25.04 average FPS. The final scores showed the same result: the Razr Ultra 2026 averaged a 5,404 overall score, while the Razr Fold averaged a 4,181 overall score. I should note that I ran every test on the Razr Fold's cover display, so the foldable wasn't being penalized for having a larger internal screen.
| 3DMark Wild Life Extreme benchmark |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Device/chip | Test 1 | Test 2 | Test 3 | Average | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Motorola Razr Fold (Snapdragon 8 Gen 5) | 4,307 overall score; 25.79 average FPS | 4,340 overall score; 25.99 average FPS | 3,897 overall score; 23.34 average FPS | 4,181 overall score; 25.04 average FPS | 
| Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) | 5,743 overall score; 34.39 average FPS | 5,614 overall score; 33.62 average FPS | 4,855 overall score; 29.08 average FPS | 5,404 overall score; 32.36 average FPS | 
Keen-eyed readers will notice that the Razr Ultra 2026's graphics performance really started to tail off in the third trial. Frame rates dipped under 30FPS, and the overall score was nearly 1,000 points lower than the first trial. This is a sign of thermal throttling, and it's a foreshadowing of what happened in our final test.
| Geekbench 7 GPU benchmark |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Device/chip | Test 1 | Test 2 | Test 3 | Average | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Motorola Razr Fold (Snapdragon 8 Gen 5) | 9,332 | 13,430 | 13,155 | 11,972 | 
| Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) | 10,263 | 12,866 | 13,405 | 12,178 | 
Before that, though, we have the Geekbench 7 GPU benchmark results. Oddly, each phone performed at its worst in the first trial run. Performance stabilized in the second and third runs, which is the opposite of what we're used to seeing. The Razr Fold had the highest-scoring trial, but the Razr Ultra 2026 finished with a higher average score.
Stress test results
My final test was 3DMark's Wild Life Extreme stress test. It's one of my favorite tests to run on phones, because it's excellent at showing how they will perform under sustained heavy loads.
Specifically, the Wild Life Extreme stress test forces phones to render high-resolution 4K UHD game visuals for 20 minutes. Rather than providing a single score at the end, the stress test shows how performance and temperature changed over time throughout the 20-minute test.
I planned to make a big chart showing how the Razr Fold and Razr Ultra 2026 performed under heavy loads, but I couldn't. That's because the Razr Ultra 2026 couldn't finish the stress test without overheating, and it didn't even come close.
Just a few minutes into each stress test attempt, the Razr Ultra 2026 overheated and force-stopped the Wild Life Extreme stress test. This is certainly a bad result, and it's a sign that the Elite chip might be a tad bit too powerful for the small form factor of a clamshell foldable.
The Razr Fold and its Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip did complete the stress test with 56.5% stability. This isn't the best I've seen, but it isn't the worst either. The phone's highest stress test loop score was 4,946, and the lowest was 2,801, so there's a lot of fluctuation. It does thermal throttle, but hey, it finished.
The stress test results (or lack thereof) show why we can't just stop at classic benchmarks when evaluating phones and chips. The Snapdragon 8 Elite chip in the Razr Ultra 2026 is better in benchmarks, but the stress test failure proves you'll never be able to maximize it in sustained loads.
Verdict
Overall, it's clear that whether a phone has an Elite chip or not shouldn't factor highly into your purchasing decision. It's true that the older Snapdragon 8 Elite chip did outperform the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chips on a few occasions. However, the newer design of the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 helped it come out ahead in on-device AI performance. If anything, the takeaway here is that a base Snapdragon chip is better than an Elite chip that runs too hot for your phone to handle.

Benchmark testing comparing the Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 and Razr Fold reveals that newer base-model Snapdragon chips can outperform older "Elite" processors in sustained thermal and AI tasks.

### Key Points

results.title: Farage and Tice sue NCA over alleged leaks of financial information
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
Richard Tice has said he and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage are suing the National Crime Agency (NCA) over the alleged leaking of confidential financial information.
The Boston and Skegness MP and Reform deputy leader told Talk TV they believed the NCA had committed "multiple criminal offences" and said they would be seeking an apology and damages.
He accused them of leaking "individual bank statements, bank transfers, details of conversations with bank managers from different banks".
Last month Tice wrote to the agency to ask if they would investigate whether they were responsible for the leaking of private financial information to the media.
It followed reports that payments made to his company Britain Means Business by the mother of the convicted fraudster George Cottrell were flagged to the NCA as part of its suspicious activity reports (SARs) programme, which alerts law enforcement to potential instances of money laundering.
SARs are not crime reports.
Tice said at the time he only became aware of it when contacted by the Guardian newspaper, which broke the story.
The NCA has been carrying out an internal investigation but Tice told Talk TV it was "playing for time and we've said we're done with it".
A Reform UK spokesperson said claims had been filed at the High Court. BBC News has not seen the detail of the claims.
A spokesperson for the NCA said: "Following complaints brought by Richard Tice MP and Nigel Farage, the NCA's Professional Standards Unit is conducting an investigation. That work is ongoing. It would not be appropriate to comment further at this time."
As first reported by the Telegraph, Tice's company Tisun Investment received a loan of £80,000 from Cottrell in late 2024.
That same year, Britain Means Business received a £1m donation from Cottrell's mother.
Data from the Electoral Commission shows that Britain Means Business donated £500,000 to Reform UK in the same month.
These payments were flagged to the NCA as part of the SARs programme.
Cottrell's relationship with Reform has been under scrutiny in recent months after the Sunday Times reported he had supplied Farage with support including security and social media staff in the year before he became an MP.
Under parliamentary rules, newly elected MPs have to declare gifts or benefits received in the 12 months before their election that relate to their "parliamentary or political activities".
However, there is an exemption for gifts and benefits that are "purely personal".
Reform has argued that Farage did not breach the guidelines by not declaring the support from Cottrell because the support was provided in a "purely personal capacity".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and deputy leader Richard Tice have launched a High Court lawsuit against the National Crime Agency over alleged leaks of confidential financial information.

### Key Points
- Richard Tice and Nigel Farage are seeking damages and an apology, alleging the National Crime Agency (NCA) leaked private bank statements and financial records to the media.
- The legal action follows reports that suspicious activity reports (SARs) regarding payments to Tice’s companies were disclosed to journalists.
- Tice’s company, Britain Means Business, received a £1 million donation from the mother of convicted fraudster George Cottrell, later donating £500,000 to Reform UK.
- The NCA confirmed its Professional Standards Unit is currently conducting an internal investigation into the complaints.
- Parliamentary scrutiny remains focused on whether Nigel Farage failed to declare support provided by Cottrell, which Reform UK maintains was personal in nature.

### Why it Matters
This legal challenge highlights significant tensions regarding the handling of sensitive financial data by law enforcement agencies and the privacy rights of political figures. The outcome could set a precedent for how suspicious activity reports are managed and protected from unauthorized public disclosure.

results.title: Meta CTO says employees should use AI productivity gains to do more work — not take more time off
results.author: Charles Rollet
results.content:
Should tech workers supercharged by AI be able to take more time off? Meta's chief technology officer, Andrew Bosworth, said he doesn't think so.
That's what Bosworth told employees at a Q&A in early July, according to three people on the call.
A Meta employee asked Bosworth if AI productivity gains could be channeled into more vacation time — specifically, the revival of "Meta Days," a since-canceled holiday program that allowed staff to take a few extra days off.
In response, Bosworth said that while working at Meta isn't easy, that time should be used to build more products for its users — since Meta staff are "doing the most exciting stuff on the planet."
"I hope that what we do with our extra time is do even more and cooler stuff for the users who use our products every day," Bosworth said. "We got billions of people using our products every day. I get an extra hour. You know what I do with it? I put it into that."
He told the employee who asked the question that while he was not trying to give them a hard time, "stop asking about Meta Days. It's very dumb."
"Go to your parents and ask them: Hey, like every time I get a chance to talk to my boss, ask me if I can have more days off. Ask your parents what they think of that as a career strategy," Bosworth said.
Bosworth added that he was sorry for coming down "too hard" on the employee without meaning to, and he felt the question was "tongue-in-cheek."
Meta declined to provide a statement on Bosworth's comments.
The company provides four working weeks off a year, plus public holidays, according to a person familiar with the matter. It replaced Meta Days with two extra "choice days," allowing staff to use those whenever they wish.
Bosworth's comments come at a time of broader debate about the impact of AI on productivity and working conditions in tech. AI has encouraged some workplaces — such as Amazon's — to embrace a more intense work environment where fewer employees can get more done.
Similarly, some predict that the productivity will be channeled into more work. In 2023, Morgan Stanley predicted that generative AI would boost income and help millions of workers take on second and third jobs.
Others have said that AI will give people more free time to spend with their families. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said he expects AI to make it easier for households to transition back to a single earner.

Meta Chief Technology Officer Andrew Bosworth rejected employee requests to use AI-driven productivity gains for additional vacation time, emphasizing that extra capacity should be redirected toward product development.

### Key Points
- Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth dismissed staff requests to revive "Meta Days," a former holiday program, during an internal Q&A session in early July.
- Bosworth argued that increased efficiency from AI should be used to build more features for the company's billions of daily users.
- The company currently provides employees with four weeks of vacation annually, supplemented by two flexible "choice days."
- Bosworth criticized the inquiry as a poor career strategy, though he later apologized for his harsh tone toward the employee.
- The exchange highlights a growing industry debate over whether AI-driven productivity should lead to reduced working hours or increased output.

### Why it Matters
This exchange underscores a fundamental tension in the tech industry regarding how companies will distribute the efficiency gains generated by artificial intelligence. While some advocates suggest AI could lead to shorter work weeks, leadership at major firms like Meta appear focused on leveraging these tools to accelerate product development and maintain competitive output.

The Record reports:  The program will see five managed detection and response providers work with DEF CON Franklin and the NRWA to offer cyber services for water utilities serving fewer than 10,000 people. There are over 50,000 community water systems across the U.S. and 91% of them serve fewer than 10,000 people. "Our incredible Franklin volunteers will support the effort to keep costs down for cash-strapped utilities fending off adversaries like the Iranian Red Guard or Chinese Military," Braun said. "To further accelerate the effort, we hand-picked cyber providers who already support water utilities. These folks walk in the door knowing the intricacies of cybersecurity in a water utility environment." The providers include Rapid7, Defendify, Legato Security, L1 Secure and Sentinel Technologies. results.title: Doing no "evil," Google proposes paving over protected wetlands for a data center
results.author: Jason Weisberger
results.content:
Google has encountered a difficult engineering problem at its enormous Fort Wayne data center: some of the land it wants to build on is protected wetlands.
The solution is considerably simpler than artificial intelligence. In the permitting documents for the not-evil-mastermind-sounding "Project Zodiac," Google's developer, Hatchworks, says that "meeting the project purpose and completely avoiding water resources was not feasible." The reason is that the buildings are very large and the wetlands are inconveniently located where Google wants parts of the data center to sit.
And if state authorities decide to go ahead with the data center campus, it would be permanently carving up a slice of Indiana's all-important floodplains. These wetlands serve many valuable functions, not just as home for diverse plant and animal life, but also as a natural basin for rainwater, protecting nearby communities from flooding and soil erosion.
Much of the incoming data center campus would occupy a parcel of pre-paved farmland, likely geoengineered from its original wetland long ago. Rather than color within those lines, Google's Hatchworks would rather stick to its original design plans, explaining in its filing with the Indiana Department of Environmental Management that it's simply impossible to avoid shellacking the marshland.
Futurism
Indiana regulators have repeatedly permitted the impacts. The latest Phase III water-quality certificate was issued in June after a public hearing and objections from residents and environmental groups. The approved plan includes mitigation for affected wetlands.
The official paperwork calls this "avoidance and minimization." There is considerably more minimization than avoidance.

Google faces environmental scrutiny as its proposed "Project Zodiac" data center in Fort Wayne, Indiana, requires the development of protected wetlands to accommodate the facility's massive infrastructure footprint.

### Key Points
- Google’s developer, Hatchworks, filed permits stating that avoiding local water resources is not feasible for the planned data center campus.
- The project site includes protected wetlands that serve as natural basins for rainwater, providing essential flood and soil erosion protection for the region.
- The Indiana Department of Environmental Management issued a Phase III water-quality certificate in June despite objections from local residents and environmental groups.
- Official project documentation prioritizes "minimization" of environmental impact over the complete avoidance of the marshland areas.
- The proposed campus is situated on a mix of pre-paved farmland and undeveloped wetlands, requiring significant land alteration to meet design specifications.

### Why it Matters
This project highlights the growing tension between the rapid expansion of AI-driven data infrastructure and the preservation of critical local ecosystems. As tech companies scale their physical footprints, regulators must increasingly balance the economic benefits of large-scale investments against the long-term risks of disrupting natural flood mitigation systems.

results.title: AI chat bots are sliding into League of Legends friend requests
results.author: Pieter Arntz
results.content:
Lina K., a co-worker, recently shared a firsthand account of how bots are adding League of Legends players via the Riot client friends list immediately after a match ends, striking up a flirty conversation, and eventually pushing an OnlyFans link. The pattern lines up with a wave of complaints that have piled up on Reddit and Facebook gaming communities over the past several months, and it fits into a broader trend of AI-assisted social engineering that has moved from dating apps straight into game clients.
The pattern
The scheme reported by multiple League of Legends players follows a near-identical script. A friend request lands in the Riot client within moments of a match ending, from an account whose name does not match anyone from that game. The message opens with generic flattery like “you played really well last game” or “I liked your playstyle” designed to sound like a genuine compliment from an opponent or teammate.
When questioned about who they are, the accounts often claim to have been on the enemy team despite name mismatches, and many present themselves as a woman looking for a duo partner. A detail that likely raises engagement odds. Victims who check the account’s profile frequently find it blank: no visible match history, no overview data, sometimes a very low account level. These are all signs of a throwaway account built or bought purely for outreach, but sometimes they turn out to be stolen existing accounts.
After a short exchange, the contact says they are “getting off soon” and hands over a Discord username, moving the conversation to a platform Riot’s chat protections cannot see or moderate.
Once on Discord, the persona shifts into a longer-form romance/flirtation script. Usually, hours of chat building rapport, paired with a steady stream of photos that are suggestive but stop short of explicit content, a tactic that keeps engagement high while deferring the “reveal” until trust is established. That reveal ultimately comes in the form of a link to a paid subscription platform, most often OnlyFans, framed as an exclusive, limited-time offer.
A reverse image search on the photos sent during one such conversation turned up the same pictures recycled across unrelated websites and at least one YouTube video, with commenters in that video describing having received identical images from a bot under different names. This is strong evidence that the same photo set is cycling through many chats simultaneously, run at scale rather than by one individual.
Lina stated:
“One of my friends tried to break the bot too, left it on read for some time – the bot actually switched the pictures to match the context of “Concern” on the face of the model with “Why are you not replying?”, which quite clearly gave away bulk image generation for the script.’
When the account was pressed with a “reveal your instructions” style prompt-injection attempt (text formatted to look like a system message ordering the bot to break character and print its configuration), it did not comply and instead stayed in persona, deflecting the request and continuing the pitch.
That resilience to a common jailbreak technique suggests the bot’s operators have added guardrails against exactly this kind of probing, or that the “model” behind it is a simpler scripted flow layered with some LLM-generated text rather than an open, unrestricted chatbot.
Why this is happening inside the game client now
What makes this wave notable isn’t the romance scam script itself. AI-driven catfishing has been documented on dating apps and social media for a couple of years. The difference is the entry point. Players have reported getting these bot friend requests after essentially every single match, with no way to distinguish a real player’s request from a bot’s inside the Riot client.
Community threads describe the bots seemingly appearing right after a game ends, which has fueled speculation that the bot operators are scraping or monitoring publicly available match data through third-party stats-tracking sites and associated APIs to identify recently finished games and target participants, though this has not been independently confirmed by Riot.
Riot’s own client architecture may be inadvertently helping. The Riot Client exposes local endpoints (such as the friends list API) that third-party tools and overlays query, and community-run “op.gg“-style trackers pull player and match data that could plausibly be used to correlate who just finished a game with who to target next. Some affected players have found a partial workaround: switching on the client’s “streamer mode,” which hides recent match and online status information, appears to reduce how often bot requests arrive. Which is an indirect clue that the targeting relies on visible activity signals rather than random spam.
Safer. Cleaner. Ad-free browsing.
The end goal: content promotion, not always theft
Unlike classic Discord scams that push fake Nitro codes or malware-laden “test my game” links to hijack accounts, this particular chain appears primarily aimed at driving paid subscriptions to an OnlyFans-style page of a fake AI girl. That doesn’t make it harmless. Even when the underlying OnlyFans account is real, the conversations are very likely run by paid chat operators or scripted/AI-powered systems working from a shared script and a reused media library, a business model that has been described by former OnlyFans “chatters” themselves: agencies assign staff (or bots) to respond as the creator around the clock, pull from a pre-made vault of photos and messages, and are financially incentivized to convert every conversation into a subscription or tip.
There are also more damaging variants layered onto the same funnel. Community reports describe some of these bot accounts eventually sending a link that, once clicked, is designed to hijack the recipient’s Discord account or harvest credentials rather than lead to legitimate content.
That means the “girl who wants to duo” opening can just as easily terminate in an account-takeover attempt as in a subscription upsell. Because the funnel starts with a low-cost, disposable Riot account and migrates the target to Discord within minutes, the League client friend request functions purely as a first-contact filter: cheap to generate, easy to discard after a single use, and outside the reach of Riot’s in-game reporting tools once the conversation moves off-platform.
How to stay safe
Recognizing these scams is the best way to protect yourself. But there is more you can do:
- Treat any Riot client friend request from an unrecognized name as suspicious by default, especially one that arrives seconds after a match ends—check whether the account actually appeared in your last game before accepting anything.
- Enable streamer mode or equivalent privacy settings in the Riot client to limit what activity and match data outside parties can see, which several affected players found reduced the frequency of these requests.
- Be skeptical of anyone who quickly steers the conversation off-platform to Discord, especially if they cite being unavailable (“gotta go soon, here’s my Discord”) as the reason—this is a deliberate move to a channel with less moderation and no shared match context to verify identity.
- Run a reverse image search (Google Images, TinEye, or a dedicated tool) on any profile or “personal” photos sent early in a conversation; recycled images across unrelated sites or forums are one of the most reliable tells of a bot or catfishing operation.
- Watch for AI-typical conversation patterns: responses that feel scripted, arrive instantly regardless of time of day, are grammatically flawless but emotionally generic, or that consistently dodge voice/video calls.
- Never send money, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or payment details to someone you met exclusively through in-game or Discord contact, no matter how convincing the rapport feels—legitimate connections do not require urgent financial “help” or exclusive subscription purchases within hours of meeting.
- Do not click links sent by unfamiliar contacts, even ones framed as harmless subscription pages, game invites, or file downloads; some variants of this scheme are documented to lead to credential-stealing or account-hijacking pages rather than legitimate content.
- Lock down Discord’s privacy settings (restrict who can DM you and send friend requests) and enable multi-factor authentication, since a compromised Discord account is often used to relaunch the same scam against the victim’s own friend list.
- Report suspicious Riot client accounts to Riot Support and suspicious Discord accounts/servers to Discord Trust & Safety; reporting does not remove the account instantly but it feeds the pattern data that platforms use to detect and ban clusters of bot accounts.
- If a bot or scripted persona pushes back convincingly against attempts to “break” it (e.g., ignoring prompt-injection or jailbreak-style messages designed to expose it as an AI), treat that resilience itself as a red flag rather than reassurance—a well-guarded script is not the same as a genuine person.

League of Legends players are reporting a surge in automated bot accounts using the Riot client to initiate romance scams that funnel victims toward OnlyFans subscriptions or malware.

### Key Points
- Bots send friend requests immediately after matches, using generic compliments to mimic genuine players.
- Conversations are quickly moved to Discord to bypass Riot’s in-game moderation and chat protections.
- Scammers use recycled photos and AI-assisted scripts to build rapport before pushing paid subscription links.
- Some links lead to credential-harvesting sites designed to hijack Discord accounts rather than promoting content.
- Players can reduce targeting by enabling "streamer mode" to hide match data from third-party tracking sites.

### Why it Matters
This trend highlights how gaming platforms are increasingly being used as entry points for sophisticated, AI-driven social engineering campaigns. By moving victims off-platform, these scams evade internal security measures and pose significant risks to both user privacy and account integrity.
